lead: This unit is about what a water jet does to a moving surface, and how that push becomes shaft power in a turbine. You will read velocity triangles, apply Euler's turbomachine equation, work out a Pelton, Francis and Kaplan wheel, size a draft tube, and finish by choosing a turbine for a given head and discharge.
about: The unit opens with 6.1, where a jet strikes a plate or a vane and the force depends on how fast the vane runs away. 6.2 packs the same physics into velocity triangles and Euler's turbomachine equation, the one formula behind every turbine and pump. 6.3 sorts turbines into impulse and reaction families, and 6.4 works the Pelton wheel in full: jet, buckets, work done and efficiencies. 6.5 repeats that for the Francis and Kaplan reaction runners. 6.6 explains the draft tube that lets a reaction turbine sit above the tailwater. 6.7 reduces every machine to unit quantities and a single number, the specific speed. 6.8 joins the efficiencies, reads the performance curves and picks the machine for a site.

chapters.idea: A jet loses momentum when a vane turns it, so the vane feels a force, and that force depends on how fast the vane moves away from the jet.
chapters.depth: Stationary flat vertical plate, stationary curved vane, moving flat plate, moving curved vane, single vane against a series of vanes. Define ρ (density, kg/m³), a (jet area, m²), V (jet speed, m/s), u (vane speed, m/s), θ (angle through which the jet is deflected). Derive F = ρaV² for a flat plate, F = ρa(V − u)²(1 − cos θ) for one moving curved vane, and F = ρaV(V − u)(1 − cos θ) for a series of vanes. Work done per second and vane efficiency. Some syllabi call this 'impact of jet on flat and curved vanes'.

figure.aria: Work rate against vane speed ratio for three vane arrangements; the single vane peaks near 0.33 and the series of vanes peaks at 0.5.

chapters.example: A jet 40 mm in diameter with V = 25 m/s strikes one curved vane moving at u = 10 m/s. The vane deflects the jet through 120° and friction is neglected. Find the force on the vane and the work done per second. Answer: a = π(0.04)²/4 = 1.257×10⁻³ m², relative speed at inlet = 25 − 10 = 15 m/s, F = ρaV_r1(V_r1 − V_r1 cos 120°) = 1000 × 1.257×10⁻³ × 15 × (15 + 7.5) = 424 N, work rate = Fu = 4.24 kW.
chapters.trap: Using the absolute jet speed V instead of the relative speed V − u for a moving vane, and dropping the (1 − cos θ) factor so a flat plate looks as good as a hemispherical cup.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: linear momentum equation. Unit 1: density and jet area.
chapters.leave: Force on pipe bends and nozzles stays in Unit 3. Bucket shape and the u = V/2 proof belong to 6.4.

chapters.idea: Every turbomachine transfers energy through the change of angular momentum of the fluid, and Euler's equation states that change in terms of the inlet and outlet velocity triangles.
chapters.depth: Draw both triangles. u = blade speed (m/s), V = absolute velocity, V_r = relative velocity, V_f = flow velocity, V_w = whirl (tangential) velocity. Euler head H_E = (u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2)/g, in metres; work per unit mass = u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2 in J/kg. Handle the sign when the outlet whirl is opposite to u₂. Degree of reaction R = share of the head that is pressure drop; impulse means R = 0, reaction means 0 < R < 1. State why a pump has the same equation with the signs reversed.

figure.aria: Inlet velocity triangle: blade speed u along the base, absolute velocity V₁ from the origin to the tip, whirl and flow components, and relative velocity V_r1 closing the triangle from the tip of u.

chapters.example: At the inlet of a runner u₁ = 20 m/s and the water enters at V₁ = 25 m/s, making 30° with the direction of blade motion. Find the whirl and flow components and the relative velocity. Answer: V_w1 = 25 cos 30° = 21.65 m/s, V_f1 = 25 sin 30° = 12.5 m/s, V_r1 = √(12.5² + (21.65 − 20)²) = 12.6 m/s. If the outlet whirl is zero, work per unit mass = u₁V_w1 = 20 × 21.65 = 433 J/kg.
chapters.trap: Getting the direction of V_w2 wrong: a negative outlet whirl makes the two terms of Euler's equation add rather than subtract. Never put V in place of V_w.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: angular momentum equation. 6.1: relative velocity over a moving vane.
chapters.leave: Pump velocity triangles, minimum starting speed and NPSH go to Unit 7. Here only turbines are taken through numerically.

chapters.idea: Turbines are sorted by how the pressure behaves across the runner, by the direction the water flows, and by the head the site offers.
chapters.depth: Impulse against reaction: in an impulse machine the whole head becomes a jet in the nozzle and the runner runs in air at constant pressure; in a reaction machine the runner is full of water and the pressure falls as the water crosses it. Flow direction: tangential (Pelton), radial, mixed flow (Francis), axial (Kaplan). Head bands: high, medium, low. Single-jet against multi-jet. Only a few universities teach this as a stand-alone topic, so keep it short: one classification tree, one comparison line, one worked pick.

figure.aria: Tree splitting hydraulic turbines into impulse (Pelton, high head) and reaction (Francis for medium head, Kaplan for low head) families.

chapters.example: A site gives H = 25 m and Q = 40 m³/s. Pick a turbine type and find the shaft power at overall efficiency 0.90. Answer: low head with large discharge suits a Kaplan turbine. P = ρgQHη = 1000 × 9.81 × 40 × 25 × 0.90 = 8.83 MW.
chapters.trap: Calling Francis an impulse turbine because it has a casing and looks enclosed, or claiming a reaction runner has no pressure change at all.
chapters.leave: Runner geometry, work done and efficiency details to 6.4 and 6.5. The specific-speed numbers that confirm the choice to 6.7.

chapters.idea: A Pelton wheel takes a high-head jet and turns it through almost 180° in its buckets, giving maximum work when the bucket speed is about half the jet speed.
chapters.depth: Parts: penstock, nozzle with spear, runner with buckets, casing, tailrace, brake nozzle. Jet ratio m = D/d, number of buckets, speed ratio φ = u/V₁ around 0.46, nozzle coefficient C_v around 0.97 to 0.99. Work done per unit weight = (u/g)(V_w1 − V_w2) with V_w2 = u − k V_r2 cos β for a bucket turned through angle β. Hydraulic, mechanical and overall efficiency. Prove that a frictionless hemispherical bucket gives maximum η_h at u = V₁/2 and the force is then maximum. Need for multi-jet units at large power.

figure.aria: Block flow of a Pelton unit: penstock, nozzle and spear, free jet, buckets, runner and shaft, with the key quantity written at each step.

chapters.example: A Pelton wheel works under H = 400 m with a 0.15 m jet, C_v = 0.98, speed ratio 0.46, bucket angle 165° and bucket friction factor k = 0.9. Find the hydraulic efficiency and the shaft power. Answer: V₁ = 0.98√(2 × 9.81 × 400) = 86.8 m/s, u = 39.9 m/s, Q = 0.01767 × 86.8 = 1.534 m³/s, V_r1 = 46.9 m/s, V_r2 = 0.9 × 46.9 = 42.2 m/s, V_w2 = 39.9 − 42.2 cos 15° = −0.8 m/s. Work per unit weight = 39.9(86.8 + 0.8)/9.81 = 356.8 m, η_h = 356.8/400 = 0.892. Shaft power = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.534 × 356.8 = 5.37 MW.
chapters.trap: Taking the bucket angle as the deflection measured from the jet direction instead of from the bucket motion, which flips the sign of V_w2 and destroys the answer.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 force on a moving curved vane. 6.2 Euler head. Unit 3: Bernoulli for the nozzle.
chapters.leave: Pelton wheels use no draft tube; that belongs to 6.6. Part-load curves to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Francis and Kaplan are reaction turbines: the runner stays full of water, the pressure falls as the water crosses it, and a draft tube recovers the leaving kinetic energy.
chapters.depth: Francis: spiral casing, stay ring, guide vanes, mixed-flow runner, draft tube; water enters radially and leaves axially, degree of reaction near 0.5. Kaplan: axial-flow propeller runner, adjustable runner blades and guide vanes, low head and large discharge. Work done from Euler's equation in both cases. Compare against Pelton on head, discharge, speed, part-load efficiency, cavitation risk and governing (guide vane opening). One worked Euler calculation is enough; keep the geometry descriptive.

figure.aria: Water path through a Francis turbine: spiral casing, stay vanes, guide vanes, runner and draft tube, with the guide vanes marked as the controlling part.

chapters.example: A Francis runner has u₁ = 20 m/s, V_w1 = 18 m/s at inlet and V_w2 = 0 at outlet. The net head on the runner is 45 m. Find the Euler head and the hydraulic efficiency. Answer: H_E = (u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2)/g = (20 × 18 − 0)/9.81 = 36.7 m. η_h = 36.7/45 = 0.816, that is 81.6%.
chapters.trap: Using the guide vane angle as if it were the runner blade angle, and forgetting that the net head on the runner is less than the gross head once draft tube and casing losses are removed.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 velocity triangles and Euler's equation. 6.1 relative velocity.
chapters.leave: Draft tube types and efficiency to 6.6. Pump impeller triangles to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A draft tube slows the water leaving the runner and turns its kinetic energy back into pressure, so the turbine can sit above the tailwater without losing that head.
chapters.depth: Why the runner exit cannot be at atmospheric pressure. Bernoulli from runner exit (2) to tailrace (3) with the runner exit H_s above the tailwater: p₂/(ρg) = p_atm/(ρg) − H_s − (V₂² − V₃²)/2g − h_f. Pressure at exit must stay above vapour pressure, which sets the maximum suction head. Types: conical, elbow, Moody spreading. Efficiency η_d = actual pressure head recovered ÷ (V₂² − V₃²)/2g, typically 0.8 to 0.9. Link to cavitation.

figure.aria: Fraction of the exit velocity head recovered against the draft tube area ratio; the ideal curve rises towards one and a real tube recovers about 85 per cent of it.

chapters.example: A draft tube of inlet diameter 0.6 m and outlet diameter 1.2 m carries Q = 1.5 m³/s, and its efficiency is 0.85. Find the velocity head recovered and the head actually recovered. Answer: A₂ = 0.283 m², A₃ = 1.131 m², V₂ = 5.31 m/s, V₃ = 1.33 m/s; (V₂² − V₃²)/2g = (28.2 − 1.76)/19.62 = 1.35 m; actual recovery = 0.85 × 1.35 = 1.15 m; head lost = 0.20 m.
chapters.trap: Writing the draft tube efficiency as a ratio of pressures instead of heads, and forgetting to subtract the exit velocity head V₃²/2g before applying η_d.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: Bernoulli's equation. 6.5: conditions at the runner exit.
chapters.leave: Cavitation and NPSH for pumps sit in Unit 7; only the turbine side is treated here.

chapters.idea: Unit quantities strip size and head out of a turbine's numbers, and specific speed puts every turbine on one scale so the type follows from a single number.
chapters.depth: Unit speed N₁ = N/√H (rpm), unit discharge Q₁ = Q/√H (m³/s), unit power P₁ = P/H^1.5 (kW), for H in metres. Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^1.25 with N in rpm, P in kW, H in m; state clearly that some books define it from discharge instead, and give the two formulas. Typical ranges: Pelton 10 to 60, Francis 60 to 300, Kaplan 300 and above. Use with unit quantities to predict a geometrically similar machine, and note the dimensionless form ω√Q/(gH)^0.75.

figure.aria: The specific speed ranges of the three turbines laid out on one axis: Pelton 10 to 60, Francis 60 to 300, Kaplan above 300.

chapters.example: A turbine develops 5000 kW at 300 rpm under H = 80 m with Q = 7.2 m³/s. Find the specific speed, unit speed and unit discharge, and name the type. Answer: √P = 70.71, H^1.25 = 80 × 80^0.25 = 239.3, N_s = 300 × 70.71/239.3 = 88.7, which is the Francis range. N₁ = 300/√80 = 33.5 rpm. Q₁ = 7.2/√80 = 0.805 m³/s.
chapters.trap: Mixing the power-based and discharge-based definitions of specific speed, and feeding P in watts or H in centimetres into a formula that wants kW and metres.
chapters.prereq: 6.4 and 6.5 for the machines being scaled. Unit 5: dimensional similarity and model laws.
chapters.leave: The Buckingham Pi proof and model testing to Unit 5. Choosing between turbines to 6.8.

chapters.idea: The four efficiencies of a turbine multiply into one overall efficiency, and the running point is where the turbine curve meets the head and discharge the site can give.
chapters.depth: Hydraulic η_h = (u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2)/(gH), volumetric η_v = (Q − leakage)/Q, mechanical η_m, overall η_o = η_h η_v η_m = shaft power/(ρgQH). Main (constant head) curves, operating (constant speed) curves, Muschel curves and the iso-efficiency hill. Why a Kaplan holds its efficiency down to part load while a Pelton falls away quickly. Selection from head, discharge, specific speed, rotational speed and cavitation limit; a word on governing and speed control.

figure.aria: Efficiency against discharge ratio for the three turbines: the Pelton peaks sharply near design flow, the Francis peaks in the middle range, and the Kaplan stays almost flat over a wide band.

chapters.example: A turbine passes Q = 5 m³/s under H = 60 m with η_h = 0.92, η_v = 0.96 and η_m = 0.97. Find the overall efficiency and the shaft power. Answer: η_o = 0.92 × 0.96 × 0.97 = 0.857. Water power = ρgQH = 1000 × 9.81 × 5 × 60 = 2.943 MW. Shaft power = 0.857 × 2.943 = 2.52 MW.
chapters.trap: Adding the efficiencies instead of multiplying them, and reading a constant-speed hill curve as if it were a constant-head curve.
chapters.prereq: 6.4, 6.5 and 6.7 for work done, losses and specific speed.
chapters.leave: Pump characteristic curves, NPSH and cavitation to Unit 7. Unit 5 covers similitude used in model testing.
